overview.text: Earth’s mantle is the mostly solid, silicate-rich layer between the thin crust and the core. About 2,900 kilometers thick, it makes up most of Earth’s interior. It is not a global ocean of molten rock: under the intense heat and pressure underground, solid mantle rock can deform and creep extremely slowly. Heat-driven movement within the mantle transfers energy toward the surface and helps drive plate tectonics, including seafloor spreading. In some hotspot models, heat rising through the mantle contributes to volcanic activity, though magma forms at shallower depths. Scientists continue to investigate the details of mantle circulation and the origins of hotspots.

key_facts.text: The mantle lies between Earth’s crust and core; the Moho marks its upper boundary, and the core–mantle boundary is roughly 2,900 kilometers below the surface.
Mantle rocks are mostly silicates, including minerals such as olivine, garnet, and pyroxene.
The mantle is mostly solid, but its rock can deform and flow very slowly under deep-Earth conditions; the asthenosphere is a relatively weak, ductile region in the upper mantle.
Mantle convection transfers heat and material; it is associated with plate tectonics and processes such as seafloor spreading.

A USGS explanation of the Hawaiian hotspot describes solid mantle rising as heat moves upward, with magma forming at shallower depths; the proposed origin of hotspots is a scientific model, not a settled explanation for every hotspot.
